newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Dlr/mark rise seen peaking 1st half '97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Dlr/mark rise seen peaking 1st half '97.

text.p: The dollar's recent rise against the mark will peak around mid-1997, then stumble below its current rate by year-end, a survey of U.S. currency analysts showed.

Fuelling the dollar will be a growing interest rate differential between the two economic powers, the approach of a proposed single European currency, and more fiscal prudence by European nations attempting to meet strict Maastricht economic convergence criteria, experts said.

A Reuter survey of 10 U.S. currency analysts showed that on average, the dollar is expected to rise from its current level of roughly 1.5520 marks to 1.5610 marks by June 1997 before falling to 1.5360 by December 1997.
"I think it is a good environment for this modest rise in the dollar to continue," said John Rothfield, international economist at NationsBanc Corp.

Last week, the dollar hit a 23-month peak of 1.5735 marks after trading below 1.50 marks less than 10 trading days prior. The dollar kicked off 1996 below 1.45 marks and first pierced the key 1.50 mark level in April.

"Moving dollar/mark higher will be persistent weakness in the European economies and movement toward prospects for a single currency in Europe, which would tend to weaken the deutsche mark and all the other European currencies against the dollar," Rothfield said.
European Monetary Union and the European System of Central Banks are both scheduled to start operating in 1999.

Politics is also expected to play a significant role, with European governments wanting the Continent's currencies to trade weaker against the dollar to boost their exports in the run up to monetary union.

"The pivotal issue is going to be the process towards monetary union in Europe and the degree to which that keeps pressure on the Bundesbank to keep rates low and political pressure within Europe to keep the dollar relatively strong," said Ron Leven, currency strategist at J.P. Morgan.

Turning to interest rates, U.S. economists expect any rise in U.S. interest rates to predate any such a move in German rates, widening the current interest rate differential and enhancing the appeal of holding dollars.

Leven and First Chicago NBD's head of international market analysis Craig Larimer expect Federal Reserve policymakers to start raising the fed funds rate in the first half of next year. They see Bundesbank officials holding the discount rate flat well into 1998 with a bias for another ease.
Experts said a relatively narrow difference in U.S. and German yields will continue to dampen foreign exchange price volatility, which was exceptionally low in 1996.
On Tuesday, the U.S. 10-year Treasury note traded at a 6.21 percent yield while its German counterpart switched hands at a 5.76 percent yield.
"I see a year in which we do get some improvement, from a bank's perspective, in volatility, but it's not going to be an excessively volatile year," Rothfield said.
"The main reason for that is capital movements may continue to be fairly uninteresting primarily because we do not have much of a yield difference between the U.S. and Germany," he added.
Working in the mark's favor, experts said, could be the promise of an unwinding of outstanding long positions in currencies of Europe's high-yield countries.

"I think the appreciation of high-yield currencies has gotten to a point that they can't stomach much more. My question is can France, Italy and Spain really benefit from a continued strengthening in their currencies against the mark? I think not," said Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney.
"That will lead to renewed flows into the mark and end up supporting a somewhat orderly mark advance," she added.
